title: witty-feather
text: We are a team of 5 trainees at EUROCONTROL in Brussels, from Spain, Italy and France, working in different units across the Agency. Our backgrounds are a mix of air traffic management, aeronautical engineering, data science and operations research, and most of us joined the Agency for a 6 months traineship directly after finishing our studies. Our motivation comes from the format of the challenge. It asks for open data, open code and a paper others can reproduce. As people at the start of an aviation data-related career, that is a rare chance to learn by comparing our work against teams from research, industry and other ANSPs, and to leave something behind that outlives our traineeship. If we finish with a model we understand, a clean repository and an honest write-up of what did not work, we will consider the challenge worth it, whatever the leaderboard says. As a group of Trainees at EUROCONTROL, we acknowledge and accept the two additional conditions: - We would not be eligible for the prize money if we end up among the top-ranked teams; and - We will not use any EUROCONTROL data, relying exclusively on the open datasets.

title: whimsical-night
text:
We are a multidisciplinary aviation and data science team from Viaratech, combining expertise in aerospace engineering, software and data engineering, machine learning, and aviation operations.
Our team brings together experience from both the aviation industry and large-scale data and technology environments. This gives us an opportunity to approach the challenge not only as a machine-learning prediction problem, but also from the perspective of the physical and operational factors that influence aircraft ground movements.
We decided to participate in the PRC Data Challenge because taxi-out time is a particularly interesting example of a highly variable aviation process where operational conditions, airport configuration, traffic intensity, aircraft characteristics and network effects interact. Developing a model that performs well across 11 major European airports therefore represents both an interesting data-science problem and a practical aviation challenge.
Our objective is to explore a transparent and reproducible modelling approach that combines aviation-domain understanding with data-driven feature engineering and machine-learning methods. We are particularly interested in understanding which operational variables explain taxi-out variability and how well those relationships generalise across different airports and operating conditions.
The challenge also strongly aligns with our interest in open aviation research. Beyond achieving a competitive prediction accuracy, we hope to produce an interpretable and reproducible methodology that contributes useful insights to the wider aviation community.

title: vigorous-x-ray
text:
Who I am. A one-person team. I hold a PhD in geoinformatics from the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, where I teach photogrammetry, laser scanning and geospatial data processing. My research has focused on managing and processing very large geospatial datasets — point-cloud data management on Apache Spark, LiDAR classification with machine learning, and spatial indexing for distributed workloads. In industry I work as a geospatial software engineer on production spatial platforms (PostGIS, raster and vector pipelines, cloud deployment). Data science, spatial processing and aviation are the three things I enjoy most, and this challenge happens to sit exactly where they meet.
Why I registered. Taxi-out time is usually modelled as a temporal problem, with the stand–runway pair treated as a categorical key. I think a good part of it is geometric: the actual taxi route from stand to runway threshold, its length, the number of turns and intersections, and the runway crossings along the way. My plan is to build a taxiway graph for all ten airports from open OpenStreetMap aeroway data, derive route-based priors from it, and measure how much they add to a solid gradient-boosting baseline with congestion and runway-configuration features. The question I want to answer, and publish either way, is whether a small, open, geodetically grounded spatial layer is worth as much as the usual temporal feature engineering.
Approach. Open data only, a reproducible pipeline, a public GitHub repository, and a short write-up for the Journal of Open Aviation Science.

title: vigorous-glove
text:
We are a team of students with a background in computing and software development, but relatively limited experience in machine learning and aviation.
We decided to join the PRC Data Challenge 2026 because we saw it as an opportunity to step outside our current skill set and learn how data and machine learning can be applied to solve a real-world problem. Rather than working only with textbook examples, we wanted to challenge ourselves with a large, real dataset and a practical prediction problem with clear operational relevance.
Our goal is not only to develop an accurate taxi-out time prediction model, but also to understand the process behind it — from exploring and interpreting the data, to identifying meaningful patterns, engineering useful features, building models and evaluating their performance.
We see this challenge as an opportunity to learn by doing, experiment with ideas, and develop skills that we can carry into future projects.

title: vibrant-jewel
text:
Outside work I’m a licensed amateur radio operator (2D0PEY), and most of my projects sit where RF, hardware and data meet. I receive ADS-B at home and built NearestPlane, an ESP32-driven display showing the closest aircraft overhead in real time. I also run a couple of small public data tools of my own, so I’m used to shipping something at the end rather than leaving it in a notebook.
Taxi-out time appealed to me because it’s a genuinely operational problem rather than a synthetic one. The interesting part isn’t the model, it’s the framing: taxi-out is largely a question of how congested the airfield is at the moment a flight goes off-block, so the work sits in representing queue state, traffic in the surrounding window, runway configuration and stand geometry. That’s a much more interesting problem than it first looks.
I registered because the combination of open data, a clearly defined target and a public leaderboard is the best possible way to test whether my intuitions about the problem actually hold up. I’m also committed to the open solutions side. Whatever I produce will go up as a documented public repository, whether or not it finishes anywhere near the top.

title: versatile-violin
text:
I’m Arnav Hemanth, a final-year Computer Science (Data Science) student at Dayananda Sagar Academy of Technology and Management in Bengaluru, India. Solo entry.
Most of what I’ve built is aviation predictive maintenance. My main project is EngineWatch (enginewatch.tech), an interpretable engine health monitoring and remaining-useful-life system trained on NASA’s C-MAPSS turbofan data. It’s deployed and running, not a notebook. The thing I care about there is that every prediction traces back to specific sensors — no deep learning, no post-hoc explanation layer sitting on top of a black box.
I registered because taxi-out is a problem I want to be better at. Engine degradation is slow and physical. Taxi-out is operational — queues, runway configuration, how an airport actually behaves at 07:00 on a Monday. Same tooling, completely different reasoning, and I’d rather learn that against a public leaderboard than on my own.
I’m also curious whether a model you can actually explain stays competitive here. That’s the position I’ve been working from for about a year and I’ve never tested it somewhere the score is public. If it holds up, I want to write it up for JOAS. If it doesn’t, that’s worth writing up too.

We look forward to taking on this challenge and producing a meaningful, data-driven solution.

title: strong-turtle
text:
My name is Ehimen Nathaniel and I’m a Nigerian. I am a data scientist and reservoir engineer participating in the PRC Data Challenge 2026 to bridge my expertise in high-dimensional predictive modeling with complex physical systems. As a reservoir engineer, I specialize in modeling pressure dynamics, fluid flows, and network bottlenecks; this physics-guided intuition translates seamlessly to predicting airport surface congestion and taxi-out times. Viewing airport taxiways as localized pipelines where aircraft are the flowing components allows me to approach this logistics problem with a unique engineering lens, utilizing advanced time-series regressions like Gradient Boosting to minimize the competition’s RMSE metric.
Participating in this challenge, backed by Europe’s Performance Review Commission (PRC) and the OpenSky Network (OSN), provides an elite platform to showcase my ability to solve real-world, high-frequency data challenges outside of the energy sector. My goal is to leverage this robust 2025 dataset of major European airport movements to secure a spot in the 5,000 EUR prize pool and ultimately publish a multi-disciplinary, open-access paper in the Journal of Open Aviation Science (JOAS).

title: smart-parrot
text: Tayte Sartorelli, independent builder in New Hampshire, USA, working with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) as a solo team. Registered to test a preregistered, fully reproducible approach to taxi-out prediction: queue and congestion features derived from the movement data itself (departures and arrivals per runway in the preceding minutes, stand-to-runway structure, time-of-day and season) plus open weather, with the evaluation protocol written down before any model is fitted. The solution will be published under GPLv3 with documentation to reproduce every submission. Motivation: learning the airport-operations domain through a well-defined open-data problem, and building a public record of open contributions (this month also the Vesuvius Challenge, with tooling pull requests to its open-source pipeline).

title: playful-anchor
text:
Solo team led by CHEN CHIEN CHANG, based in Taiwan. Professional background in airline operations, including flight dispatch, fuel planning, trajectory analysis and airport performance. Combining operational knowledge of taxi, departure sequencing and airport capacity with data analysis and applied machine learning.
Registering to build an open, reproducible model of taxi-out time at the 11 challenge airports. Taxi-out time affects block time, fuel burn, stand occupancy and departure punctuality, yet planning still often uses schedule or average values that miss configuration, traffic intensity and runway in use. The intended approach is to start from transparent operational baselines, then add supervised models with documented features. Code and any additional open datasets will be released under GNU GPLv3 so results can be reproduced, in line with the challenge conditions.

title: motivated-ostrich
text:

I decided to take part in the PRC Data Challenge to put my experience to the test on a new and challenging problem. I am motivated by the opportunity to push the limits of my current skills, explore new approaches, and learn from the challenge. I also see it as a great opportunity to apply the knowledge I have gained through my previous projects in a competitive and practical environment.

title: motivated-dolphin
text:
I am Abdourahamane Idé Salifou, an AI engineering student . I am especially interested in applying machine learning to optimization problems, where a model has to turn messy operational data into a prediction that can improve a real decision.
In December 2024 I placed first in the Abidjan Mobility Prediction Hackathon, powered by Yango on Zindi, predicting average traffic speed on Abidjan’s main roads. I joined the PRC Data Challenge 2026 to take that interest into aviation: predicting taxi-out time at 10 major European airports from open 2025 movement data, ranked by RMSE. Taxi-out time depends on layout, traffic, schedule and operations, so a better estimate can support tighter planning of departures, stands and runway use. My goal is developing a strong AI solution aiming to improve the operation itself fewer uncertain departures, tighter use of stands and runway time, and less delay not only to produce a score for leaderboard .

title: knowledgeable-forest
text:
I am a recent Computer Science graduate with experience in software engineering, open-source development, and machine learning projects. Alongside technology, aviation has been one of my strongest personal interests. I enjoy learning about aircraft such as the Airbus A350 and Boeing 777, following airline operations, tracking flights, and understanding how airports and air traffic systems work.
I decided to join the PRC Data Challenge because it brings together two areas I genuinely enjoy: aviation and machine learning. Predicting taxi-out time is particularly interesting to me because it requires both technical analysis and an understanding of real airport operations. Factors such as aircraft type, runway configuration, departure queues, traffic levels, and time of day can all influence the result.
Through this challenge, I hope to strengthen my skills in exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, time-based validation, and predictive modelling while working with large-scale, real-world aviation data. I also aim to produce an open and reproducible solution that clearly explains both the model and the operational factors behind its predictions.

title: happy-caterpillar
text:
stand-by is a one-person team: Georgios Stavropoulos, a researcher based in Thessaloniki, Greece, participating in a personal capacity. My day-to-day work is applied machine learning and data engineering on European collaborative research projects, mostly on messy real-world operational data rather than clean benchmarks.
I registered because taxi-out time is a genuinely hard prediction problem hiding inside a very ordinary-looking tabular dataset: the signal lives in airport congestion, queueing at the runway, stand-to-runway geometry and time-of-day effects rather than in any single column. That is exactly the kind of problem I enjoy - most of the work is in constructing the right features from context, not in tuning a model.
My aim is to build a well-documented, fully reproducible baseline and iterate on queueing and congestion features, and to share the whole pipeline openly on GitHub regardless of where it lands on the leaderboard. If the results are interesting enough, I would like to write them up for the Journal of Open Aviation Science.

title: genuine-avocado
text:
Who I am
I’m Nitesh, an independent data scientist and engineer with a background spanning computer vision, geospatial intelligence, voice AI, RAG/LLM systems, and cloud infrastructure. I graduated from IIT Delhi and have spent the past few years building end-to-end ML pipelines and offline-first data platforms for real-world, field-deployed applications — working with noisy, high-frequency sensor and operational data, and turning it into reliable predictive systems.
Why I’m registering
I have a long-standing personal interest in aviation and flight tracking. I previously built SkyWatcher, a web app that pulls live ADS-B data to show a flight’s speed, altitude, and path on an interactive map — a project born purely out of curiosity about how much can be reconstructed about an aircraft’s behavior from open flight data. Taxi-out time prediction feels like a natural extension of that interest: it’s the kind of messy, real-world operational data problem with genuine downstream impact (fuel burn, emissions, delays) that I enjoy working on. I’m also motivated by the challenge’s open-data and open-science ethos — publishing code publicly and writing up the approach for JOAS mirrors how I already like to work, having co-authored papers on applied ML pipelines before. This felt like a great opportunity to combine my aviation curiosity with my modelling and engineering skills, benchmark myself against a strong community of practitioners, and contribute something useful back to the open aviation research ecosystem.

title: dynamic-lobster
text:
Who I am
Saurabh Nandedkar, an engineer based in Mumbai, India, working in applied ML and infrastructure. Outside work I run an AIS receiver station tracking vessel traffic, and I’m setting up an ADS-B station next — partly to feed back into the networks I take data from.
Why I registered
Two reasons.
The first is that I already spend my spare time on the receiving end of this kind of data. Running an AIS station teaches you quickly how much of the interesting signal is in what the raw messages don’t say — gaps, timing, and the state of the world you have to infer around them. Taxi-out is the same shape of problem. The movement records tell you when things happened, not what was happening on the surface; the work is reconstructing runway queues, sequencing and configuration from timestamps alone. That’s the part I want to do.
The second is the open-science framing. Open data, public code, and a paper at the end is the right shape for a competition. I’d rather spend a month on something that leaves a public artifact behind.
How I’m approaching it
Solo, in Python. Gradient boosting over engineered features rather than anything exotic — I expect the work to live in feature construction and validation design, not model architecture. Planning month-disjoint splits given that the ranking months sit at both extremes of the year, and bringing in open weather data for the winter cases. Code goes on GitHub regardless of where I place.

title: Rationale
text:
The choice of predicting taxi-out time for this year’s Data Challenge builds on previous challenges, which have focused on using data to better understand environmental and operational impacts.
Taxi-out time is particularly interesting because it is often difficult to obtain and challenging to predict accurately.
A model to estimate taxi-out time can be used in post-operations analysis to identify constrained operations intervals and measure excess fuel burnt/CO2 production compared to unconstrained status.
The reasons for variability of taxi-out time are various and interlinked. These include airline-specific constraints, airport procedures and load, and Air Traffic Flow Management (ATFM)-related reasons.

title: PRC Data Challenge 2026
text:
The Performance Review Commission (PRC), with the support of OpenSky Network (OSN), invites data scientists, aviation professionals and data analysts to collaborate and compete in a data challenge to develop innovative methodologies for benefit of the broader aviation community.
The aim is to do this through:

title: PRC Data Challenge 2026
text:
Data Challenge
The 2026 edition of the PRC Data Challenge invites participants to predict the taxi-out time of flights from 10 major European airports.

Scope
The learning dataset will consist of all 10 airport movements for the full year of 2025.


Ranking
The applied ranking will use Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) for submitted predictions for the movements in January and July 2026.


Timeline
The competition runs from the \(1^{st}\) of September 2026 up until the \(11^{th}\) of October 2026 23:59:59 CET.






ImportantImportant



We are having a final submission for which the deadline is 2026-10-14T12:00 CET (2026-10-14T12:00+02:00)




Reward
The combined prize amount for the first 3 teams is 5000 EUR.


Terms & Conditions
Check the Terms & Conditions for eligibility for participation and prize before filling in the team creation request form.






NotePlease note



We reserve the right to change the rules or even stop the challenge due to any circumstances.




Participate
Join the competition; request the creation of your team here!

Request Team Creation!







ImportantImportant



Your request will be assessed by the PRC Data Challenge team for approval. Upon approval you will receive a verification email and, on successful reply, the relevant access keys to the datasets/buckets.
Note: The participation is open to all, but teams from sanctioned countries are excluded.

title: PRC Data Challenge 2026
text:
Outreach
We are strong advocates of open science and (strongly 😉) encourage teams, particularly the top-ranked teams, to submit a paper to JOAS describing their approach and the inner workings of their models.
Here are some examples from previous editions:

Open Machine Learning Models for Actual Takeoff Weight Prediction
A Physics-Guided Gradient Boosting Framework for Open-Source Aviation Fuel Estimation

We also publish a data paper describing the challenge dataset, with the aim of making the data more accessible and supporting further use in research, education, and other applications.
Examples from previous editions include:

Aircraft Fuel Burn Estimation: The EUROCONTROL PRC 2025 Data Challenge
Aircraft Takeoff Weight Estimation: The EUROCONTROL PRC 2024 Data Challenge

The following GitHub organizations host the repositories of participating teams:

2024 teams’ repos, https://github.com/prc-data-challenge-2024
2025 teams’ repos, https://github.com/prc-data-challenge-2025

title: Data
text:
Column Description
Columns postfixed with _mvt are associated with the reporting airport.
Columns postfixed with _flt are associated with information from NM flight list.

Movement

MVT_ID_mvt: unique identifier for the movement record
FLIGHT_ID_mvt: unique identifier for the NM flight (if matched)
FLIGHT_mvt: flight number, i.e. what you see on your boarding pass
FLIGHT_RULE_mvt: which sets of regulations the flight is operated under. Possible values are:

I for Instrument Flight Rules (IFR)
V for Visual Flight Rules (VFR)
NA if unknown

ADEP_mvt: the (ICAO code of the) Aerodrome of DEParture (ADEP).
ADES_mvt: the (ICAO code of the) Aerodrome of DEStination (ADES).
PHASE_mvt: movement phase. DEP=departure, ARR=arrival.
MVT_TIME_UTC_mvt: (best available) movement time (takeoff if PHASE = DEP, landing if PHASE = ARR.)
BLOCK_TIME_UTC_mvt: block time (off-block if PHASE = DEP, in-block if PHASE = ARR.)
SCHED_TIME_UTC_mvt: scheduled time (of departure if PHASE = DEP, of arrival if PHASE = ARR.)
AIRCRAFT_TYPE_mvt: the ICAO code for the aircraft type, for example A21N for Airbus A321neo.
RUNWAY_mvt: the Runway (RWY) ID (of departure if PHASE = DEP, of arrival if PHASE = ARR.)
STAND_mvt: the stand ID (of departure if PHASE = DEP, of arrival if PHASE = ARR.)
TAXITIME_SEC_mvt: amount of seconds for taxi time (taxi-out if PHASE = DEP, taxi-in if PHASE = ARR.)



Flight
The following columns come from data recorded by NM.

LOBT_flt: last known off-block time
CALLSIGN_flt: the callsign of the relevant flight, e.g. BAW6VB.
ADEP_flt: the ICAO code of the ADEP.
ADES_flt: the ICAO code of the ADES.
ADES_FILED_flt: the ADES initially filed in the Flight Plan (FPL). If different from ADES_flt, then the flight has been diverted.
MARKET_SEGMENT_flt: the market segment type as defined in the Market Segment Rules, it can be:

“Mainline”
“Regional”
“Low-Cost”
“Business Aviation”
“All-Cargo”
“Charter” (Non-Scheduled)
“Military”
“Other”
“Not classified”

IOBT_flt: Initial Off-Block Time (IOBT).
FLIGHT_RULE_flt: which sets of regulations the flight is operated under (see FPL Item 8). Possible values are:

I for IFR
V for VFR
Y first IFR thereafter VFR
Z first VFR thereafter IFR

FLIGHT_TYPE_flt: flight type (see FPL Item 8). Possible values are:

S for scheduled air service
N for non-scheduled air service
G for general aviation
M for military (note: filtered out)
X for other than the preceding categories

AIRCRAFT_TYPE_flt: the ICAO code for the aircraft type, for example A30B for an Airbus A-300B2-200.
WK_TBL_CAT_flt: wake turbulence category (see FPL Item 9), can be:

L LIGHT, i.e. maximum certificated takeoff mass of 7000 kg (15_500 lbs) or less.
M MEDIUM, i.e. maximum certificated takeoff mass less than 136_000 kg (300_000 lbs), but more than 7_000 kg (15_500 lbs).
H HEAVY, i.e. maximum certificated takeoff mass of 136_000 kg (300_000 lbs) or more (except those specified as J).
J SUPER, presently only the AIRBUS A-380-800.

AIRCRAFT_OPERATOR_flt: the (anonymized) ICAO Airline Designator.
EOBT_1_flt: the Estimated Off-Block Time (EOBT) for FPL-based (M1) trajectory.
ARVT_1_flt: the arrival time for FPL-based (M1) trajectory.
AOBT_3_flt: the Actual Off-Block Time (AOBT) for flown (M3) trajectory.
ARVT_3_flt: the arrival time for flown (M3) trajectory.

title: Eligibility
text:
NotePlease note



We have made every effort to ensure that the registration process complies with the applicable eligibility rules. However, we reserve the right to refuse/stop participation of teams from countries/companies subject to restrictions at any stage of the challenge.

title: Eligibility
text:
Eligibility for participation
Participation is open to teams worldwide, subject to applicable sanctions and restrictions.
Restrictions apply to teams originating from, or affiliated with, institutions or companies in countries that are either not EUROCONTROL Member States or Comprehensive Agreement States, or are subject to sanctions.
Regardless of the reason for the sanctions, these restrictions are also in place because of the practical difficulties involved in transferring prize money to winning teams based in these countries.
The registration form implements these restrictions as far as possible.
Please refer to the EU Sanctions Map and to the EUROCONTROL Member and Comprehensive Agreement States for the list of EUROCONTROL states.

title: Eligibility
text:
Eligibility for Prize
The winning submissions/solutions will only be eligible for the awards if:

The team is NOT related in any way to sanctioned non-EUROCONTROL states. See above.
All used external datasets are openly accessible/usable and documented.
All produced source code are made openly available on GitHub under the GNU GPLv3 license. Note: It will then be forked by the Challenge GitHub account for organisational purposes.
All additional datasets used are openly available under an open source license.
Sufficient documentation is provided to understand and reproduce the results.
The solution is original: Teams must use their own original solutions. Re-using any existing implementation is only allowed if the original authors grant you the rights to use their solution and if you made significant modifications to the algorithm or model. In particular, simply re-using existing code and rewriting the data input and output mechanism is not sufficient. Adding parameters to the model and modifying filters to match the specific peculiarities of the data, however, can be considered sufficient.
Final single submission is uploaded by 2026-10-14T12:00 CET (2026-10-14T12:00+02:00)

title: Ranking
text:
Submission Instructions
Teams will be ranked based on the best Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) achieved across their submissions.
The submitting.parquet file is provided as a template. To make a submission, fill in the TAXITIME_SEC_mvt column with your predicted taxi-out times for the corresponding MVT_ID_mvt values.
Each team must submit its predictions to its own bucket using the following file naming convention:

<team-name>_v<incremental integer>.parquet

For a submission to be valid, each row must match the corresponding MVT_ID_mvt before the ranking script can use the prediction to calculate the RMSE.
The ranking script will issue an error if:

an MVT_ID_mvt does not match;
any rows are missing; or
extra rows are included.

There is currently a limit of 5 submissions per day (and a total max of 1GB per bucket.)






NotePlease note



You will NOT be able to submit via the webinterface, please use the MinIO CLI as described in the Data section.

title: friendly-strawberry
text:
I am Morris Maina, a Data Scientist and aviation enthusiast based in Nairobi, Kenya, with a background in machine learning, data analytics and aviation-focused predictive modelling. My work sits at the intersection of data and real-world operational problems, with a particular interest in using machine learning to improve how aviation systems anticipate and respond to disruption.
I decided to participate in the PRC Data Challenge because taxi-out time is a problem where data science can have a direct operational impact. It is influenced by traffic demand, airport capacity, runway operations, weather and the constantly changing state of the airport surface. That makes it both technically challenging and highly relevant to aviation.
I am particularly interested in understanding whether machine learning can move beyond simply predicting taxi-out time to identifying the operational conditions that cause excessive taxiing and congestion. I hope to build a model that is accurate, explainable and grounded in how airports actually operate.
The challenge also provides an opportunity to contribute to aviation research while learning from a real-world European ATM dataset. As someone developing aviation intelligence solutions, I see this as an opportunity to deepen my understanding of airport surface operations and explore ideas that could eventually support more proactive decision-making in aviation.

title: humble-jacket
text:
I am Andreas Hadjinicolaou, a computer science student at the University of Cyprus, entering my final year. I am entering on my own rather than as part of a research group or a company.
I registered because taxi-out time is the kind of problem I want more practice on: real operational data, a metric nobody can argue with, and a held-out period that settles the question. Most public datasets I have worked with are either toy problems or financial series where almost everything is noise. Airport surface movements are neither, and the drivers are physical and schedulable rather than random.
The other reason is how this challenge is run. Previous editions publish every team’s code and the write-ups go to an open journal, so the work stays useful after the deadline. That is uncommon in data competitions and worth supporting.

title: jolly-napkin
text:
We are a two-person team combining backgrounds in Computer Science and Aerospace Engineering / Air Traffic Control (ATC). One of us is a Computer Science student focused on machine learning and scalable data pipelines, while the other brings domain knowledge as an aerospace engineer and current ATC trainee with a deep interest in ATM efficiency.
We registered for the PRC Data Challenge 2026 because predicting taxi-out times sits precisely at the intersection of our skill sets. Accurately modeling ground congestion, airport surface dynamics, and pushback-to-takeoff delays presents a realistic, high-impact operational challenge. We are strongly aligned with the challenge’s open-science mission and look forward to developing robust, open-source models on OpenSky Network data and contributing our solution to the broader aviation research community.

title: jubilant-puzzle
text:
The team south-wind is a solo project run by a data analyst with several years of experience in data analytics and machine learning. After working in larger tech hubs, the participant now lives in Haikou, a coastal city on the south coast of Hainan Island, China, and works locally. The name “south-wind” comes from this setting: doing aviation research from a small coastal city in the south, where the south wind blows year-round.
The team joined the PRC Data Challenge 2026 for three reasons:

To learn and sharpen skills in time-series regression and gradient boosting modelling. Predicting taxi-out time is a concrete, well-scoped problem that is ideal for practising feature engineering, time-series validation and ensemble methods.
To contribute to open aviation research. Even if the final ranking is modest, the team plans to release all code and notes under an open licence so that future participants can build on this work.
To do something useful and a bit different. Aviation operations have real-world impact on emissions and passenger experience, and being able to predict taxi-out time even roughly is genuinely useful. Working on it from the south wind side of the world is the team’s small way to participate in open European aviation research.

The team will work primarily in Python, using XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost as the main models, with feature engineering focused on time-of-day, congestion patterns and aircraft-specific factors.

title: logical-ladder
text:
We are a multidisciplinary team of four students bringing together three Computer Science students and one Avionics student, with a shared interest in artificial intelligence, data science, aviation and building technology that can solve real-world problems.
Our Computer Science members contribute skills in programming, machine learning, data analysis and model development, while our Avionics member brings an aviation and aircraft-systems perspective that helps us understand the physical and operational context behind the data. As a team, we also have an entrepreneurial mindset through our experience in building technology projects and developing a startup, which has taught us to approach technical problems not only from the perspective of “Can we build it?” but also “Can it work in the real world, and can it create meaningful value?”
This combination is particularly relevant to the PRC Data Challenge. Taxi-out time is not simply a mathematical prediction problem; it is influenced by aircraft, airport operations, traffic and other interconnected operational factors. The challenge therefore gives us an opportunity to combine our different areas of expertise rather than treating data science and aviation as separate disciplines.
We see ourselves as students who are still learning, but who are eager to work on problems where advanced technology, engineering and real-world operational data meet.
We decided to participate in the PRC Data Challenge 2026 because it gives us the opportunity to apply artificial intelligence and data science to a genuine aviation problem rather than working only with classroom or synthetic examples.
This year’s challenge focuses on predicting aircraft taxi-out time using real operational data from major European airports. The problem is particularly interesting to us because taxi-out time is affected by multiple interacting factors, making it a meaningful machine-learning problem with a direct connection to aviation operations. EUROCONTROL notes that better prediction of taxi-out time can help identify periods of constrained airport operations and support the assessment of excess fuel burn and CO₂ emissions associated with those conditions.
For our team, the challenge is also an opportunity to bring together our different backgrounds. Our Computer Science members can work on data processing, feature engineering, machine-learning models and evaluation, while our Avionics member can contribute aviation-domain understanding. Our entrepreneurial experience motivates us to look beyond simply producing a prediction and to think about how data-driven insights could eventually support more efficient aviation operations.
We are participating to challenge ourselves against an international community, learn from a real-world aviation dataset, strengthen our ability to build reproducible AI solutions, and explore how our combined technical backgrounds can be applied to problems with practical significance.
Ultimately, we see the PRC Data Challenge as a bridge between what we learn as students and the kind of data-driven engineering problems we hope to solve professionally.

title: merry-quicksand
text:
Independent researcher working on operational forecasting for aviation from open data. I run a live, continuously published forward record of GNSS interference built from open ADS-B integrity signals, scored daily against independent sources, with each forecast cryptographically timestamped before its outcome is known.
Taxi-out is the same problem in a different layer — a short-horizon operational forecast over open trajectory data, where the difficulty is proving the evaluation is honest rather than fitting the model. I am registering to test that methodology against an external scoreboard and to contribute the leakage-control tooling back openly.

title: merry-scooter
text:
I am a data engineer based in Vilnius, Lithuania, registering as an independent participant. My day to day work is building data pipelines and working with APIs over large operational datasets, and I hold a degree in IT.
I registered because taxi-out time is the kind of problem I like working on: a clearly defined regression target on real operational data, with enough structure in the movement records, and in the open weather and flow management data the challenge allows, that the modelling choices actually matter. Most public datasets available to practise on are either toy sized or long since solved. This one is neither, and it is scored on a held out period rather than a random split, which makes the evaluation honest.
I intend to publish my code and documentation in a public repository whatever my final placing, and to write up the method if the result turns out to be worth reading.

title: optimistic-radio
text:
We are a small data science team with experience in machine learning, big data analytics, feature engineering, and the development of reproducible data-driven solutions.
We decided to join the PRC Data Challenge because taxi-out time prediction combines several areas we are particularly interested in: large-scale operational data, temporal and congestion-related patterns, interpretable machine learning, and real-world decision support. We are especially interested in reconstructing latent airport surface congestion from historical movement patterns and operational features, and in evaluating how much these signals can improve taxi-out time prediction across different airports and seasonal conditions.
Beyond the leaderboard, we value the open-science nature of the challenge. Our goal is to develop an original, reproducible methodology, openly share the resulting code and documentation, and, if the results are strong enough, contribute the findings to the broader aviation research community through an open-access publication.

title: quick-witted-yarn
text:
I am an Aerospace Engineering Master’s student participating as a solo data scientist. title: resilient-kiwi
text:
I am Stephen Thorne, based in Johannesburg. Twenty five years in enterprise technology, most of it spent persuading other people’s data to behave itself, and these days I run AI and data science at group level. I am Group CTO for AI and Data Science at White Pearl Technology Group, a Nasdaq First North listed Swedish AI and data science group.
I registered because taxi-out time is the kind of problem I actually enjoy. It is bounded, it is measurable, and there is nowhere to hide ; the RMSE either comes down or it does not. No steering committee is going to rescue a bad model.
I am not an air traffic management specialist, which I am choosing to treat as an advantage rather than a confession. I come at it as a data person looking at a genuinely messy operational signal. Ground movement, weather, stand allocation, the queue at the holding point, and all of it out in the open where anyone can check the working.
The open science side matters to me as well. Public repo, published method, results other people can pull apart. Far too much of what I do sits behind an NDA. This does not, and that is refreshing.
And honestly, I want to know whether the instincts still hold up against a leaderboard.

title: resourceful-horse
text:
Who we are
I’m Abhishek Patil, a Data Science and Applications undergraduate at IIT Madras, currently interning as an AI/ML engineer at Fincepta. I’m competing solo under the handle zeroday19. My background is in distributed ML systems, GPU inference optimization, and forecasting on time-series and tabular data, most recently as a Kaggle Gold Medalist (11th of 1,711 globally) in the MITSUI&CO. Commodity Prediction Challenge and a Silver Medalist in the Jane Street Real-Time Market Data Forecasting Competition.
Why I registered
Flight-level operational data is a different beast from the market and commodity data I usually work with: different noise structure, different physical constraints, different failure modes. I registered for the PRC Data Challenge to stress-test my forecasting and feature-engineering toolkit (Polars pipelines, LightGBM/TabM ensembles, drift-aware modeling) on a domain I haven’t already built intuition for.
What I’m hoping to get out of it
A model I’m proud of, plus a sharper understanding of how fuel efficiency and emissions modeling works in aviation, a domain where good predictions have a real environmental impact. It’s also a chance to add another solid result to a track record built on Kaggle and quant-research competitions.

It taught me how IOBT, EOBT and AOBT actually behave, and that taxi duration in Berlin follows the distance from runway exit to stand more than it follows traffic load. Taxi-out is the half of the problem I never had to predict, and I want to see whether that physical reasoning survives across eleven different airports.

title: vibrant-lollipop
text:
I am a recent Marmara University graduate, I work as a researcher in aviation, and I have started a master’s degree. I build software across a range of domains. I am taking part on my own, not on behalf of my employer.
I will be straightforward about why I registered. I am early in my career and this is a chance to test myself in public, on a problem from my own industry, against people who do this well. The prize and the recognition that follows a good result matter to me and I see no reason to pretend otherwise. The paper matters for a separate reason: research is what I do and what I want to keep doing, so a challenge that ends in open code and an open-access publication fits where I am heading. Taxi-out is also one of the few problems where a better model turns directly into less fuel burned.
What I intend to deliver: a faithful reimplementation of EUROCONTROL’s own additional taxi-out time reference, a model for what remains on top of it, and an honest account of the approaches that failed alongside the ones that worked. The code will be public under GPLv3 and I plan to write the result up for JOAS.

title: wise-fossil
text:
We are a team of professionals from China Unicom with backgrounds in digital technology, data platforms, AI applications, and software engineering. While aviation is not our primary field of expertise, we share a strong interest in applying data-driven and machine learning methods to real-world operational problems.
We decided to join the PRC Data Challenge because it provides a valuable opportunity to work with large-scale, real-world aviation data and to explore a practical prediction problem with clear operational relevance. The taxi-out time prediction task is particularly interesting to us because it combines data analysis, feature engineering, machine learning, and domain understanding.
Through this challenge, we hope to learn more about aviation operations, strengthen our practical skills in data science and predictive modelling, and explore how different technical approaches can improve prediction accuracy. We also see the competition as a good opportunity for cross-disciplinary teamwork, experimentation, and learning from the wider data science and aviation communities.
Our goal is not only to achieve a competitive result, but also to build a reproducible and well-documented solution and gain practical experience that can be applied to other complex data-driven optimisation problems.

I am a Computer Science graduate from Concordia University with a strong interest in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and applied software systems. My previous work and projects have involved machine learning, autonomous AI agents, prediction models, and the evaluation of AI systems. I am particularly interested in problems where machine learning must work with large-scale, noisy, real-world data rather than only clean benchmark datasets.
I decided to register for the PRC Data Challenge because it combines several areas that I want to develop further: large-scale data analysis, feature engineering, predictive modeling, and understanding complex operational systems. Predicting aircraft taxi-out time is especially interesting because the problem is influenced by many interacting factors, including airport congestion, runway and stand configuration, flight schedules, aircraft characteristics, and operational conditions.
My goal in this challenge is not only to achieve a competitive prediction score, but also to better understand the underlying factors that drive taxi-time variability. I am interested in exploring how airport traffic patterns and operational information can be transformed into useful predictive features, and how different machine-learning approaches generalize across airports and time periods.
I also see the challenge as an opportunity to strengthen my ability to build a complete and reproducible machine-learning pipeline, from exploratory data analysis and feature engineering to model validation, error analysis, and final prediction. More broadly, I hope to gain practical experience applying machine learning to a real transportation and aviation problem with potential implications for airport efficiency, fuel consumption, and environmental performance.

I am especially interested in exploring the data, testing different approaches, and understanding which factors have the biggest impact on taxi-out time prediction.
My goal is to build a simple, reproducible solution, learn from the process, and enjoy the challenge.
